title: Use one specific piece of feedback without instant rebuttal

sections.title: Understand the distinction
sections.body: Feedback can contain an observation, an interpretation and a proposed remedy. Confirm the observation before accepting the remedy, and retain the listener’s actual correction rather than assuming understanding.

sections.title: Complete fictional practice material
sections.body: Original directions: “The box is near the desk; after returning the key, collect it. The key comes from the staffed desk.” Listener task: collect the empty blue box from shelf A, then return the borrowed key to the staffed desk. Fictional listener says “I cannot tell what I should do first.” The authorized task order above is complete; no real building visit is required.

sections.title: Work through the supplied case
sections.body: Summarize the feedback, identify the order problem and rewrite the directions. Save the revised wording before inspecting the follow-up.

sections.title: Try a different case before checking
sections.body: Feedback says “your date was wrong” but the dated source confirms it. Must receptivity require accepting the correction?

checks.title: Compare reasoning and review the supplied result
checks.body: “Collect the empty blue box from shelf A, then return the key to the staffed desk” fits the supplied task. Later fiction: listener confirms the order is clear but asks which shelf in another room; that new room is not supplied and remains unknown. Partial: sympathize without fixing the order. Incorrect: argue that detail proves clarity or invent a shelf for the new room.

checks.title: Check the changed case
checks.body: No. Check both sources respectfully and identify the discrepancy. Receptivity means examining evidence, not automatic agreement or a defensive claim that all feedback is useless.
